# Nobody Ever Says No

*A storyline for the hiring-team kickoff — what applying to us feels like from the other side of the portal.*

---

## Meet Maya

Maya has a job. That is the first thing to understand about her, because it changes everything that follows.

She is mid-career, competent, and quietly done with where she is. She is not unemployed and desperate; she is employed and hopeful, which means every single thing she does about our role happens in the margins of a day that already belongs to someone else. Lunch breaks. The train. Nine-forty at night, laptop on the kitchen table, after everything else is finished.

She finds our posting on her phone, somewhere in a gap.[^1] Thirty seconds of skimming, a small lift of interest — *this could actually be a good fit.*

Then she reads it properly, and the lift turns into arithmetic. Ten bullets. She's solidly got seven. Two are close. One is somebody else's job entirely.[^2] She does what people like Maya do with a list like that: she starts building the case against herself. Somewhere in the country tonight, several excellent candidates are talking themselves out of us, and we will never know their names.

Maya doesn't. Maya decides she's worth the evening.

---

## Act One: The Toll Booth

She taps Apply, and we hand her to somebody else.

The page changes shape and color — our careers site was ours, and this one belongs to a vendor she's never heard of.[^3] Before she can see a single question, it wants an account. Email, password, the rules about the password, the confirmation email, back to the tab.[^4]

She has not yet been asked one thing about herself and she has already been asked to file paperwork with a stranger.

Then the form. She uploads her resume — the good one, the one she keeps current — and watches our parser take it apart and put it back together wrong. Her last job title lands in the wrong field. Two years of a career get compressed into a blank. So Maya spends the next forty minutes typing, by hand, into small boxes, the exact document she has already given us.[^5]

Think of a restaurant that asks you to hand over your recipe, then makes you read it aloud, one ingredient at a time, while the kitchen writes it down again.

At 10:20 she reaches the end and hits Submit. And here is the thing worth noticing: **she feels good.** Relief, a little pride, the specific satisfaction of a hard thing finished.[^6] That is the emotional high point of this entire journey, and it happens forty-three minutes in, with everything still ahead of her.

---

## Act Two: The Reader She Isn't Told About

An email arrives almost immediately. *We've received your application.* No name, no timeline, no next step.[^7]

What the email does not say is that within twenty-four hours, before any human being opens it, an algorithm will read her application and decide whether a human ever will.[^8]

It scores her against the role criteria. If she misses, she gets a rejection the next morning and never learns that the decision was automated, or which criterion she missed, or whether it was a genuine mismatch or the same parser that mangled her job title in the first place.[^9]

And here is the part that should make the room uncomfortable: the applicants this machine is worst at reading are exactly the ones we say we want to reach. Career breaks. Non-linear paths. People whose experience doesn't arrive in the standard shape.[^10] We built a filter that is most confident about the candidates who look most like the last ones.

Maya clears it. She never knows it was there.

---

## Act Three: The Silence

This is the part I want us to sit in.

Maya has passed. Her application is now in a queue, waiting for a recruiter, who is waiting for a hiring manager, who has a shortlist to review behind four things more urgent than reviewing a shortlist.[^11]

Nothing about that is unreasonable. Hiring is slow because hiring is hard.

But from the kitchen table, none of it is visible. The portal says *Submitted.* Days later, the portal says *Submitted.* Her status inside our system does change — a recruiter opens it, a note gets added, it moves — and not one of those changes is ever shown to her.[^12] We know things about Maya's application that we simply do not tell her.

So the story she has is the only one available: nothing is happening, and it's probably about her.

She checks. She checks again. She drafts a follow-up email and deletes it, because following up might read as pushy, and then she sends it anyway, and it isn't answered.[^13] Eventually she finds someone from the company on LinkedIn and messages a stranger — which is not a workaround anybody designed, it's what people do when the front door has no bell.[^14]

Hope curdles into anxiety, anxiety flattens into resignation. Six weeks in, she stops checking.

Put the two numbers next to each other, because they're from the same map: **forty-three minutes of doing, inside about six weeks of elapsed time.**[^15] Roughly one part in a thousand of Maya's experience of us is the part anyone designed. The rest is her, waiting, filling the silence with her own conclusions.

---

## Act Four: Three Doors and a Wall

The journey has three real endings, and one non-ending.

She gets a rejection — weeks late, a form letter, no feedback. Disappointing, but it closes. Closure turns out to be worth something.[^16]

She gets a call, and the story continues somewhere else entirely: elation, validation, the best day of her month.[^17]

Or she gets nothing. Ever. No rejection, no closure, no event that ends the journey.[^18] The application doesn't conclude; it just runs out of Maya. She is left to work out for herself that it's over, and she will remember that we were the company that couldn't be bothered to say no.

Look at the map and that third ending isn't an edge case sitting off to the side. It's a step with **no way out of it** — every other step leads somewhere, and that one leads nowhere. Ghosting isn't a failure of the process. On this map, ghosting *is* the process, running to completion.

---

## What I want us to carry out of this room

One picture: a competent person at a kitchen table at ten at night, forty-three minutes into the good version of herself, who will hear nothing back from us for six weeks and will conclude, correctly, that we never intended to tell her anything.

Two of the three worst moments cost us almost nothing to fix. We are not being asked to hire faster — the hiring manager's shortlist is going to take as long as it takes. We are being asked to *say what is happening*: surface the status we already have, tell people an algorithm read their application and give them one chance to correct it, and sweep closed roles so that "no" always eventually arrives.

The wait is unavoidable. The silence is a choice we are currently making.

---

### A note on sourcing

This storyline dramatizes our current journey map for the online application experience. Every step, emotion, and pain point above is recorded in that map as our working understanding — **authored from internal knowledge of the flow, not from interviews, analytics, or cited research.** No drop-off rate appears here because the map holds none; the "several excellent candidates talk themselves out of us" framing is a hypothesis worth testing, not a measurement.

The two time figures are the exception, and they are honest in a specific way: **forty-three minutes** and **six weeks** are computed from the map's own `duration` and `waitTime` fields — but those fields are themselves estimates written in conversation, not instrumented. Treat the *ratio* as the finding and the digits as a bet worth measuring.

[^1]: Discovery — *see-the-posting*: found on a phone, in a gap between other things; ~30 sec skim.
[^2]: Discovery — *read-and-assess-fit*: `failureMode` — talks herself out of applying ("I only meet 7 of 10 bullets"); `painPoint` — inflated requirement lists.
[^3]: Application — *click-apply*: `channelTransition` — employer-branded careers page hands off to a third-party ATS with different branding and conventions.
[^4]: Application — *create-account*: `painPoint` — account gate before she has seen the form; `failureProbability: high`, `priority: must-fix`.
[^5]: Application — *fill-application-form*: `dataFlow` — parse errors propagate into a record she never sees; `duration: ~20-40 min`; `cognitiveLoad: high`; `emotionValence: -2` (the low point of the acting half).
[^6]: Application — *submit-application*: `emotionValence: +1`, the journey's high point; `valueExchange` — 40 minutes of unpaid labour and a full personal data record, in exchange for a confirmation screen.
[^7]: The Wait — *receive-confirmation*: `message` / `tone` — templated, no timeline, no next step, no name.
[^8]: The Wait — *ai-resume-screen*: `lineOfVisibility` — Maya is never told this step exists; `automation` — no human review on the reject path.
[^9]: The Wait — *outcome-fast-rejection*: `painPoint` — no feedback on why, and no disclosure that an algorithm decided.
[^10]: The Wait — *ai-resume-screen*: `inclusionConsideration` and `risk` — criteria proxies encode bias at scale; non-linear careers and career breaks score worst.
[^11]: The Wait — *wait-in-silence*: `handoff` (Recruiter → Hiring Manager) and `bottleneck` (hiring-manager review capacity).
[^12]: The Wait — *wait-in-silence*: `lineOfVisibility` — internal status changes exist and are deliberately not exposed; `orchestration: none`.
[^13]: The Wait — *check-status-or-follow-up*: `failureMode` — follow-ups go unanswered; `effort` — high emotional cost, near-zero information gain.
[^14]: The Wait — *check-status-or-follow-up*: `workaround` — messages an employee on LinkedIn to get any signal at all.
[^15]: Computed across the map's `duration` and `waitTime` fields; see the sourcing note above.
[^16]: Resolution — *outcome-rejection*: `emotionValence: -1` — "disappointment, but closure is its own relief."
[^17]: Resolution — *outcome-advance*: `emotionValence: +2`; continues into a separate map.
[^18]: Resolution — *outcome-ghosted*: `failureMode` — the journey ends by exhaustion rather than by any decision being communicated; the only step in the map with no outgoing path.
